Java Memory, Objects & References
1.1 Stack vs Heap
- Stack: Each thread has its own call stack, containing method frames and local variables.
- Heap: Stores objects and arrays. Objects can be shared between threads through references.
- Reference: A value that identifies an object, not a raw memory pointer.
User u1 = new User("Adam");
User u2 = u1;

u2.name = "Sara";

System.out.println(u1.name); // Sara


Rule: Both references refer to the same object.
1.2 Java is always pass-by-value
static void change(User user) {
    user.name = "Youssef";
    user = new User("Sara");
}

User u1 = new User("Adam");
change(u1);

System.out.println(u1.name); // Youssef


Java copies the reference when passing an object to a method.
- user.name = ... mutates the shared object.
- user = new User(...) only changes the method's local reference.
Remember: Reassigning a parameter doesn't change the caller's reference.

Section 02 — Strings, Equality & Hashing
2.1 == vs equals()
String a = "Java";
String b = "Java";
String c = new String("Java");

System.out.println(a == b);      // true
System.out.println(a == c);      // false
System.out.println(a.equals(c)); // true


- == compares primitive values or object identity.
- equals() uses the class's equality implementation.
- String literals are interned and can share an object.
2.2 String Pool and intern()
String a = new String("Backend");
String b = a.intern();
String c = "Backend";

System.out.println(a == b); // false
System.out.println(b == c); // true


intern() returns the canonical pooled String reference. It doesn't modify the original String.
2.3 equals() and hashCode()
import java.util.Objects;

class User {
    private final Long id;

    User(Long id) {
        this.id = Objects.requireNonNull(id);
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object obj) {
        if (this == obj) return true;

        if (!(obj instanceof User other))
            return false;

        return Objects.equals(id, other.id);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hashCode(id);
    }
}


The contract:
Condition	Meaning
a.equals(b) == true	Hash codes must be equal
Same hash codes	Objects aren't necessarily equal
Different hash codes	Objects cannot be equal if the contract is respected

Hash collisions happen when different objects generate identical hash codes.
2.4 HashSet and collisions
@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return 42;
}


Even if all objects return 42, HashSet can store multiple objects if equals() says they're different.

A HashMap bucket can contain multiple entries, commonly organized as linked nodes, and may be treeified under certain conditions.
2.5 Mutable HashMap keys
Map<User, String> map = new HashMap<>();

User user = new User("adam"); // Assume mutable username-based key
map.put(user, "ACTIVE");

user.username = "sara";

// The changed hash may make normal lookup fail.


Changing a field involved in hashCode() while the object is a key can make the entry difficult to retrieve.

Backend rule: Prefer stable, immutable keys, such as a user's immutable database ID.

Section 03 — HashMap & ConcurrentHashMap
3.1 HashMap
Map<Long, String> map = new HashMap<>();

map.put(1L, "Adam");
map.put(2L, null);


- Not thread-safe for unsynchronized concurrent modifications.
- Allows one null key and multiple null values.
- Uses hashCode() and equals() for key lookup.
3.2 ConcurrentHashMap
ConcurrentHashMap<Long, String> cache =
    new ConcurrentHashMap<>();


- Supports concurrent access.
- Does not allow null keys or null values.
- Provides atomic operations such as putIfAbsent() and computeIfAbsent().
But this is not atomic as a whole:
if (!cache.containsKey(1L)) {
    cache.put(1L, "ACTIVE");
}


Two threads may both see that the key is absent.
3.3 putIfAbsent() vs computeIfAbsent()
// Value is evaluated before the method call
cache.putIfAbsent(1L, loadUser(1L));

// Value is computed only when needed
cache.computeIfAbsent(1L, id -> loadUser(id));


	putIfAbsent()	computeIfAbsent()
Accepts	Value	Function
Lazy computation	No	Yes
Existing non-null mapping	Preserved	Preserved
Existing null mapping in HashMap	Can be replaced	Can be replaced
Computation returns null	Depends on map and supplied value	No new mapping

If a mapping function throws an exception, computeIfAbsent() propagates it and doesn't establish the new mapping.

Backend example: Lazy user-cache loading.
User user = cache.computeIfAbsent(
    userId,
    id -> repository.findById(id).orElse(null)
);


This handles lazy loading, but not cache expiration, stale entries, or every kind of database failure.

Section 04 — Java Concurrency Essentials
4.1 What is a thread?
Thread = Worker executing instructions.

Thread pool = Office managing workers.

Threads in the same JVM can access shared heap objects, but each thread has its own execution stack.
4.2 Race condition
int count = 0;

void increment() {
    count++;
}


count++ is not atomic.

Conceptually:
READ → ADD 1 → WRITE


Two threads can both read 0 and both write 1, losing an increment.
4.3 volatile
private volatile boolean running = true;


Provides visibility and ordering guarantees.

It doesn't make compound operations such as count++ atomic.
4.4 synchronized
private int count = 0;

public synchronized void increment() {
    count++;
}


A thread must acquire the monitor lock before executing the synchronized method.

This provides mutual exclusion and visibility when threads coordinate using the same lock.
4.5 AtomicInteger
AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0);

count.incrementAndGet();
count.addAndGet(10);

System.out.println(count.get());


Atomic operations safely update one integer without requiring an explicit synchronized block.
4.6 Choosing the right mechanism
Situation	Suitable mechanism
Shared boolean status flag	volatile
Shared integer counter	AtomicInteger
Protect multiple related operations	synchronized
Highly contended counter	Consider LongAdder

Important: Atomic individual operations don't automatically make an entire business transaction atomic.

Section 05 — CAS (Compare-And-Set)
5.1 What is CAS?
CAS means:
Update the value only if it still equals the value you expected.

AtomicInteger balance = new AtomicInteger(1000);

boolean first = balance.compareAndSet(1000, 700);
boolean second = balance.compareAndSet(1000, 500);

System.out.println(first);        // true
System.out.println(second);       // false
System.out.println(balance.get()); // 700


The second CAS fails because the balance is no longer 1000.
5.2 CAS retry loop
public boolean withdraw(int amount) {
    if (amount <= 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException();
    }

    while (true) {
        int current = balance.get();

        if (current < amount)
            return false;

        int updated = current - amount;

        if (balance.compareAndSet(current, updated)) {
            return true;
        }

        // Retry because another thread changed balance
    }
}


This protects the condition and update together, assuming balance is an AtomicInteger and all modifications follow compatible atomic rules.

Remember: CAS failure means the observed value changed, not necessarily that the business operation failed.

Section 06 — Threads, Thread Pools & Executors
6.1 start() vs run()
Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName());
});

worker.run();   // Executes on calling thread
worker.start(); // Starts a separate execution thread


- start() starts a new thread.
- Directly calling run() is an ordinary method call.
- You cannot call start() twice on the same thread.
6.2 ExecutorService
ExecutorService executor =
    Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);

executor.submit(() -> System.out.println("Task A"));
executor.submit(() -> System.out.println("Task B"));
executor.submit(() -> System.out.println("Task C"));

executor.shutdown();


The pool has up to two active worker threads. Additional submitted tasks wait when both workers are occupied.
6.3 shutdown() vs shutdownNow()
executor.shutdown();


Stops accepting new tasks while allowing submitted tasks to complete.
executor.shutdownNow();


Attempts to interrupt running tasks and returns tasks that never started. It doesn't guarantee immediate termination.
6.4 execute() vs submit()
executor.execute(() -> doWork());


Returns void.
Future<Integer> future =
    executor.submit(() -> 10 + 20);

System.out.println(future.get()); // 30


submit() returns a Future, which can represent a task result.

future.get() blocks the calling thread until the result is available.

Section 07 — Platform Threads vs Virtual Threads
7.1 Platform threads
Thread thread = new Thread(() -> doWork());
thread.start();


Traditional Java threads backed by operating-system threads.
7.2 Virtual threads (Java 21+)
Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> doWork());


Lightweight threads managed by the JVM, scheduled onto carrier platform threads.
7.3 Virtual-thread executor
try (ExecutorService executor =
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

    executor.submit(() -> {
        Thread.sleep(1000);
        return "DONE";
    });
}


Useful when managing many concurrent I/O-bound tasks.
Platform threads	Virtual threads
Dedicated OS thread	Share carrier threads over time
Relatively expensive	Lightweight
Commonly reused in pools	Commonly created per task
General execution	Especially useful for I/O-bound workloads

Virtual threads don't make CPU calculations faster and don't remove the need for thread safety.
